newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU edges closer to ban Boeing deal.
newsitem.headline: EU edges closer to ban Boeing deal.

text.p: The European Union, resisting growing U.S. pressure, maintained a united front on Friday in its determination to ban a merger between Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp.

The top aides of the 20 commissioners who make up the EU executive endorsed a draft decision to prohibit the deal on the grounds that it would harm fair competition in Europe, one of the aides told Reuters.
He said Boeing, which made its last offer on Tuesday, had failed to respond to a request to make new proposals aimed at meeting Commission concerns and heading off a ban.
The commissioners are now expected to make a final decision at their regular meeting next Wednesday.
Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, who has ferociously opposed the merger from the start, needs only a simple majority in the Commission for the decision to be approved.
Commission sources said a last-minute agreement was still possible, although unlikely, as the Europeans refused to soften their position in the face of U.S. pressure.

They said U.S. lobbying was intensifying in the EU's larger states, particularly in Britain whose special relationship with Washington was given fresh impetus when Labour's Tony Blair took over as prime minister.
"Britain is under very strong pressure and so are France, Italy and Germany," an EU diplomat said.
"They (British officials) may be quaking at the knees and there may be others who fear retaliation, but the procedure is under way. The Commission has competence to take a final decision."
A spokesman for Britain's Department of Trade and Industry said it did not have a position on the merger as this was a matter for the Commission.

President Bill Clinton raised the possibility on Thursday that the United States might go to the World Trade Organisaton or impose sanctions if the EU blocked the $14 billion merger, but he said a trade war could probably be avoided.
On the European side, French President Jacques Chirac argued that the deal was "extremely dangerous" for Europe and expressed concern that some of his EU partners might not resist the U.S. pressure.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl urged European aerospace firms to consolidate in response to the competitive threat from the planned merger.
"I think that Europe must give a very clear answer to the American challenge in the aerospace sector by founding its own large concern," Kohl told a news conference.

Aerospatiale of France, which is state-controlled, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and British Aerospace BAe are the main partners in the Airbus Industrie consortium, Boeing's only serious rival. European consolidation depends mainly in changing Airbus into a limited company.

BAe and its European partners have accused the U.S. commercial aircraft industry of enjoying cross-subsidies from U.S. military contracts -- one of the sticking points in the negotiations between the EU and Boeing in the merger with McDonnell Douglas.

Boeing has offered to report regularly to the EU on any cross-subsidies from McDonnell-Douglas' military business to its own civilian operations, but German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said this was not enough.

The other unresolved Commission competition concerns regard Boeing's exclusive supply contracts with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines and a perceived danger that Boeing would automatically replace McDonnell commercial aircraft in fleets worldwide.
